meta.note: All figures provisional and subject to revision by the issuing statistical office.

markets.name: United Kingdom
markets.commentary: Third rise in a row, to 3.5% from 3.1%, and 0.4% in the single month against no change a year ago. Motor fuels are still the main driver: 29.8% higher than a year ago, up from 23.0%, with petrol at 169.5 pence a litre after an 8.2 pence jump in the month, the highest since August 2022. The change from August is in the underlying measures. Core rose to 2.8% from 2.6% after three months flat, services went to 3.7% from 3.4% on air fares and goods to 3.2% from 2.7%. Restaurants and hotels were the only large offset. The pipeline kept filling too. Output prices rose 0.8% in the month and the annual rate went to 4.6%, the highest since April 2023, from a revised 3.8%. Input prices are up 8.3% from a revised 6.7%, with crude oil inputs 14.0% dearer in the month and refined petroleum outputs up 9.1%. ONS says both producer series are still being distorted by the Middle East conflict.

markets.name: Euro Area
markets.commentary: Up to 3.8% from 3.2%, unchanged from the 2 October flash and 0.6% in the month. Energy again did most of it: 18.9% year on year against 14.3% in August and 4.0% in the single month, contributing 1.71 points of the 3.8%. Services added 1.52 points as the annual rate came back up to 3.2% from 3.0%. Core (excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco) rose to 2.5% from 2.4%, so the August dip has reversed. Food, alcohol and tobacco went to 1.3% from 1.1%, while non energy industrial goods slipped to 1.1% from 1.2%. The August producer prices, the latest published, are the sharp part of the picture: up 1.9% on the month and 8.2% on the year, from 5.8% in July, with energy up 5.6% in the month and 21.0% year on year. Excluding energy producer prices are rising 3.4%.

markets.name: United States
markets.commentary: Headline rose 0.6% in the month after 0.4% in August and the annual rate went to 3.7% from 3.4%. Gasoline rose 9.1% and accounted for over half of the monthly rise; energy overall rose 5.2% and is 20.4% higher than a year ago, with gasoline up 34.2%. Core rose 0.3% for a second month and the annual core rate went to 2.6% from 2.4%, so the underlying rate has stopped falling. Shelter picked up to 0.4% and airline fares rose another 1.2%, now 22.4% above a year ago. The producer side is the larger move. PPI final demand rose 1.3% in the month, the biggest since March 2022, and the annual rate went to 6.3% from 5.4%, the highest since December 2022. Final demand goods rose 2.6% with energy up 10.8% and gasoline up 20.3%, and the measure excluding food, energy and trade services is up 5.0% on the year.

markets.name: Japan
markets.referenceDate: September 2026 (CPI published 23 October; PPI = CGPI, preliminary; CPI monthly rates seasonally adjusted)
markets.commentary: The run of 1.9% readings has ended. Headline CPI rose to 2.1% from 1.9% and the measure excluding fresh food to 2.1% from 1.7%, the first reading above the Bank of Japan's 2% target in nine months. The core measure here, excluding fresh food and energy, jumped to 2.4% from 1.9%, the highest since March, and rose 0.5% on the month seasonally adjusted. Fresh food actually pulled the headline down as its annual rate fell to 2.1% from 6.0%. Food excluding fresh rose to 2.9% from 2.7% and hotel charges swung to +4.6% from -1.4%. Energy is still 0.6% cheaper than a year ago, and the Statistics Bureau puts the drag from the gasoline tax abolition and other subsidy policies at 0.82 points of the headline. On the producer side CGPI fell 0.3% in the month for the second month running and the annual rate eased to 6.8% from 7.6%. Agriculture, forestry and fishery products fell 8.8%, mainly rice and pork, and petroleum and coal products fell 2.2%. Contract currency import prices rose 1.0% in the month, led by LNG and naphtha. Unlike the other markets, the monthly CPI rates for Japan are the seasonally adjusted ones in the release.

euroMembers.name: Germany
euroMembers.note: HICP up to 3.3% from 2.9%, the highest since December 2023 on the national CPI, which is also 3.3%. Energy accelerated for a third month to 14.9% from 10.5%. Motor fuels are 37.1% dearer than a year ago, up from 27.7%, and heating oil is 74.9% higher. Household electricity (-5.5%) and gas (-2.8%) are still held down by federal measures. The renewed fuel discount only started on 1 October, so it is not in these figures. Core stayed at 2.4% for a third month and services slowed to 2.7% from 2.8%. Producer prices for August rose to 4.6% from 3.1% and are well above consumer prices.

euroMembers.name: France
euroMembers.note: HICP to 3.4% from 2.6%. The 0.3% fall on the month is seasonal: services dropped 1.4%, with accommodation down 15.0% and transport down 9.8%. INSEE puts the seasonally adjusted national CPI up 0.8% in the month. National CPI is 3.1%, revised up a tenth from the provisional 3.0%. Energy went to 21.3% from 16.7%, with diesel up 44.1% and heating oil up 64.6%. Core rose to 1.5% from 1.1% and services to 2.4% from 1.9%, helped by accommodation prices swinging to +4.9% from +0.7% and air fares to +10.0% from +1.7%. France still has the softest core of the four. Producer prices for August at 4.8%, up from 3.5%.

euroMembers.name: Italy
euroMembers.note: The Eurostat and Istat HICP figures now agree: 4.2% year on year and 2.1% on the month, up from 3.2% in August (Istat's provisional estimate was 4.1%). The mismatch flagged last month is gone. On the national NIC index inflation went to 4.2% from 3.3%, 0.7% on the month. Energy is again the driver: regulated products 25.8% from 18.6% and non regulated 22.5% from 17.0%. Unprocessed food rose to 5.5% from 3.8%. Core edged up to 1.6% from 1.5%. Producer prices for August are the highest of the four at 13.5%, up from 9.3%, with a 3.1% rise in the month.

euroMembers.name: Spain
euroMembers.note: Still the highest of the four. HICP rose to 5.0% from 4.6% and national CPI to 4.9%, the highest since February 2023, 0.3% on the month. Transport went to 10.5% from 9.5% on fuels, which rose and then fell in September last year, and on air fares falling less than a year ago. Package holidays also fell less than in 2025 and pushed recreation to 3.6%. Unlike last month, core did not ease: it rose two tenths to 3.1%, the highest of the four. Producer prices for August at 13.2%, up from 9.3% and close to Italy.

euroMembersNote: Headline HICP year on year and month on month are both on the comparable Eurostat basis (final September 2026 release, published 16 October). Eurostat and Istat now report the same Italian HICP, so last month's reconciliation caveat no longer applies. Core measures come from each national office and are not identical: Germany is CPI excluding food and energy, France is INSEE underlying inflation, Italy is NIC excluding energy and unprocessed food, Spain is CPI excluding unprocessed food and energy. PPI is held at August 2026 for all four so it stays comparable with the euro area aggregate (+8.2%), which is the latest published month; the September euro area figure is due in early November. On that August basis: Germany +4.6%, France +4.8%, Italy +13.5%, Spain +13.2%.

signals.title: Core has stopped falling
signals.observe: Last month none of the core measures in this file went up. This month seven of the eight did and Germany was flat. Euro area core went to 2.5% from 2.4%, UK to 2.8% from 2.6%, US to 2.6% from 2.4%, Japan to 2.4% from 1.9%, France to 1.5% from 1.1%, Italy to 1.6% from 1.5% and Spain to 3.1% from 2.9%. Services rose in the UK (3.7% from 3.4%), the euro area (3.2% from 3.0%) and France (2.4% from 1.9%). UK goods went to 3.2% from 2.7%.
signals.why: Part of it is narrow. Air fares are carrying services in the UK, France and the US, where airline fares are 22.4% above a year ago, and Japan's jump has a hotel charges swing in it. But the UK goods move and the rise in euro area food suggest energy costs are starting to reach other prices. It is not broad yet: euro area non energy industrial goods slipped to 1.1% from 1.2% and German core is flat.
signals.action: Drop any line that says underlying inflation is falling. The August case for resisting repricing on cost pressure does not hold this month. The October core and services prints in November are the test: if services keep rising, treat energy as second round pressure rather than a one off.

signals.title: The energy shock got bigger and the producer data says it is not finished
signals.observe: Euro area energy is 18.9% year on year, from 14.3%. US gasoline rose 9.1% in the month and energy is 20.4% higher over the year. UK petrol hit 169.5 pence a litre, the highest since August 2022. German heating oil is up 74.9% and French energy 21.3%. On the producer side US PPI rose 1.3% in the month, the biggest since March 2022, UK output prices are up 4.6%, the highest since April 2023, and euro area August PPI jumped to 8.2% from 5.8%. Japan is the exception: CGPI fell 0.3% and eased to 6.8% from 7.6%, and consumer energy prices there are still 0.6% lower than a year ago.
signals.why: Three of the four markets moved the same way on producer prices for a second month, which points to crude and refined products rather than local policy. UK refined petroleum outputs rose 9.1% in a single month and US final demand energy rose 10.8%. Japan is being held down by policy, not by cheaper energy: the Statistics Bureau puts the gasoline tax abolition and subsidy effect at 0.82 points off the headline, and contract currency import prices rose 1.0% in the month.
signals.action: Build Q4 and 2027 energy and freight assumptions off September levels, not August. Do not read an October fall in German energy as a turn: the motor fuel discount only started on 1 October. Treat Japan's softer CGPI as provisional until the November release.

signals.title: The gap between producer and consumer prices is widening in the West and narrowing in Japan
signals.observe: Last month the producer to consumer gaps were UK 0.6 points, US 2.0, euro area 2.6 and Japan 5.7. This month UK output prices (4.6%) sit 1.1 points above CPI (3.5%), US PPI (6.3%) is 2.6 above CPI (3.7%) and euro area PPI (8.2%, August) is 4.4 above HICP (3.8%, September). Japan went the other way: CGPI at 6.8% against CPI at 2.1% is a 4.7 point gap, down from 5.7, because producer prices fell and consumer prices rose. Italy and Spain are the widest national gaps at 13.5% and 13.2% producer inflation against 4.2% and 5.0% on the HICP.
signals.why: Producers pick up crude and refined products first and at higher weight than consumer baskets. The euro area gap is slightly overstated because PPI is a month behind the HICP. Even allowing for that, the direction is the same in every Western market and the pipeline is filling faster than it is emptying. Japan is the first market where the gap is closing from both ends.
signals.action: Assume some of the August and September producer increases reach consumer prices over the next two quarters, with Italy and Spain the most exposed. Japan is still the widest gap and the one to price conservatively, but its direction has turned: the gap is now closing through falling CGPI and rising CPI at once.
